title: La Rocca's closing remarks on Brown and credit for Black jazz
summary: La Rocca says Brown's death spared him, and claims white band leaders were defamed with Black culture credited as Armstrong's.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, this case was going to go on, and probably that's what shorted Mr. Tom Brown's life, I'm sorry that happened, because he was better to me to live, than to hook him in his lies, than it was for him to die, a little bit faster, because he knew he wouldn't be able to face the lies he's made, with the help of these prophets who write on jazz, who sell periodicals, who give the wrong dope out on all kinds of stuff that they put out, they don't put anything that is truthful, they get men like Tom Brown, Arnold La Cana, fill them up with a little juice down there, then they start talking, they print what they say, why don't they come out and put their name to something like this, that's what they should do, that's what the lawyer was looking for him, Tom Brown had no money, and if I had to sue everybody, had no money, I wouldn't be able to feed my children, and maintain a house, it's easy to tell lies on a person, backed by, what you call exploiters of this music, and men who have formed syndicates, jazz clubs, societies, and whatnot, to defame one man, all because he was the leader, of the first jazz band in the world, and it happened to be a white band, and they want to give this culture to the Negro, who was not around until eight, ten years after, and if, Louis Armstrong hadn't been born, the Negro never had, would have been knowing about jazz, because it was him, he would get the credit, for bringing the colored man, into the picture of jazz, the others couldn't do it, they didn't have it, they say they had it, when you can listen to their records, you change your mind, I see this tape running out, and I'm trying for time, to put everything I can get on there,
